identification.summary: REF2924 is Elastic Security Labs' name for an activity group (intrusion set) that Elastic observed using the C# HTTP-listener implant NAPLISTENER, which Elastic describes as built to evade network-based detection, against victims in southern and southeastern Asia [S1][S2]. Elastic reported that the group shifted from data theft toward maintaining persistent access [S1]. Elastic links NAPLISTENER to the developers of the SIESTAGRAPH implant [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Elastic's NAPLISTENER write-up (published March 2023) describes a service binary installed on 2023-01-20 [S1]. Earlier REF2924 activity (SIESTAGRAPH, an ASEAN foreign ministry intrusion) was reported by Elastic but its publication date was not verified here.
identification.notes: REF2924 is an Elastic cluster name; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is mapped in this record. Elastic's later REF5961 report says its samples were found alongside REF2924 and that EAGERBEE shows string-format and behavioral resemblance to LuckyMouse (APT27, Emissary Panda) work [S4]. That is a similarity noted by Elastic, not a merge of the clusters; do not treat REF2924 as APT27.

attribution.confidence: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered for REF2924 itself. For the related REF5961 set, Elastic assesses the operators as state-sponsored and espionage-motivated, with a China nexus based on overlapping tooling, infrastructure and victimology [S4].
attribution.basis: Elastic's technical overlap statements between REF2924, REF5961 and LuckyMouse tooling [S4]. No government attribution found.

objectives: Elastic describes the group's tradecraft as moving from data theft toward persistent access, implying a long-term collection posture [S1]. Specific tasking is not stated in the sources gathered.

targeting.notes: Elastic says the group is primarily active in southern and southeastern Asia, where network- and log-based detection is common [S1]. Elastic associates SIESTAGRAPH with a foreign ministry of an ASEAN member state, and the REF5961 report describes a foreign ministry victim in an ASEAN member state [S4].

capabilities.summary: NAPLISTENER is a C# HTTP listener installed as a Windows service named Wmdtc.exe, imitating the legitimate Msdtc.exe [S1]. Elastic says it appears built to evade network-based detection, as SIESTAGRAPH and related tools seem to be [S1].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed regional group tracked by Elastic as REF2924; developers of SIESTAGRAPH and NAPLISTENER per Elastic [S1]. Sponsor not stated.
diamond.capability: NAPLISTENER HTTP-listener implant [S1]; SIESTAGRAPH is a related implant from the same developers per Elastic [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Windows service persistence on victim hosts with a listener on the victim's own web stack; actor infrastructure not detailed in sources gathered [S1].
diamond.victim: Organizations in southern and southeastern Asia, including an ASEAN foreign ministry [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional government intelligence collection is plausible but not stated by sources; unverified.
diamond.technology: Windows and Exchange-style web servers; defenders relying on network and log detection are the specific target of the evasion design [S1].

gaps: Could not open Elastic primary pages (WebFetch DNS failure); details come from search summaries of Elastic pages and press coverage.

Publication dates for Elastic's SiestaGraph and 'Update to the REF2924 intrusion set' posts were not verified, so they are not cited as sources. Search summaries say the update assesses with moderate confidence a regional group with non-monetary motives; confirm in the original.
No sponsor, no Microsoft/MITRE mapping, no victim sectors beyond government confirmed.
Relationship between REF2924, REF5961 and LuckyMouse/APT27 is similarity only; not resolved.
A Malpedia catalogue entry for NAPLISTENER was dropped because it carries no date; the YARA rule it lists should be taken from the Elastic publication.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing Windows web services and government mail infrastructure in southern and southeast Asia are key terrain [S1][S4]. STEP 2: The actor designs implants to evade network and log based detection, so host telemetry matters [S1]. STEP 3: Template is implant installed as a lookalike Windows service (Wmdtc.exe) with an HTTP listener that blends with normal web traffic [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued persistent access to regional government networks. MDCOA is use of the persistent footholds to support coalition-partner disruption or collection during a crisis. Candidate indicators: services named Wmdtc.exe, HTTP listeners on unexpected URL prefixes, YARA Windows.Trojan.NapListener hits [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: share the Elastic YARA rule and service-name indicators with partner-nation cyber contacts in the region [S1]. (2) Authorities: partner-network hunting requires host-nation consent; no US government attribution exists to rely on. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize host-based service and listener auditing on mission-relevant web servers. (4) Coordination: attribution is unresolved; coordinate naming with vendors before reporting up.
